subject: physics

items.q: A lamp and a fixed resistor are connected in series with a cell. An ammeter placed between the cell and the lamp reads 0.30 A. A second ammeter is placed between the lamp and the resistor. What does the second ammeter read?
items.correct: 0.30 A, because in series there is the same current through each of the components
items.misconception: Less than 0.30 A, because some of the current is used up inside the lamp
items.why: Students hear that a lamp 'uses' electricity and transfer that to the current rather than to the energy carried by the charge. Charge is not used up: the charge that enters a component leaves it again. What is transferred is energy, shown by the potential difference across the lamp, not the current.
items.random_wrong: 0.15 A, because the current from the cell is shared between the two parts

items.q: A 6 V battery is connected in series with two identical lamps. A voltmeter across the first lamp reads 3 V. What does a voltmeter across the second lamp read?
items.correct: 3 V, because the supply potential difference is shared between the two lamps
items.misconception: 6 V, because each component in series has the full supply potential difference
items.why: The parallel rule, that the potential difference across each component is the same, is applied to a series circuit. Full supply potential difference across each component is the parallel rule. In series the separate potential differences add up to the supply value.
items.random_wrong: 0 V, because the first lamp has already used up the potential difference

items.q: A 4 Ω resistor and a 6 Ω resistor are joined in series. What is the total resistance of the pair?
items.correct: 10 Ω, found by adding the two resistance values together
items.misconception: 2 Ω, found by taking the difference of the two values
items.why: Combining two numbers is remembered as a vague instruction, and subtraction is chosen once the answer 'feels' as if it should be smaller. The specification gives R_total = R_1 + R_2 for series. Resistances in series add, so the total is always larger than either separate resistance.
items.random_wrong: 5 Ω, the value that lies midway between the two resistors

items.q: The specification gives the equation R_total = R_1 + R_2. Which statement does this equation express?
items.correct: The total resistance of two components in series is the sum of each resistance
items.misconception: The total resistance of two components in parallel is the sum of each resistance
items.why: R_total = R_1 + R_2 is memorised as the rule for all combinations, without noticing that it is stated only for series. Adding applies to series only. In parallel the extra branch gives charge another route, so the pair opposes the current less than either resistor alone.
items.random_wrong: The total resistance of two components in series is set by the larger resistor alone

items.q: A student is writing a key for a circuit table. Which line gives the quantity, its symbol and its unit for resistance as the specification states them?
items.correct: Resistance, symbol R, measured in ohms, for which the unit symbol is Ω
items.misconception: Resistance, symbol Ω, measured in units called R, put after the value
items.why: The quantity symbol and the unit symbol are learnt as a pair without noting which is which. R is the quantity symbol used in equations such as R_total = R_1 + R_2; Ω is the symbol for the unit, the ohm, that the value is measured in.
items.random_wrong: Resistance, symbol R, measured in volts, whose unit symbol is V

items.q: Two lamps of different resistances are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. A voltmeter across the first lamp reads 12 V. What does a voltmeter across the second lamp read?
items.correct: 12 V, since the potential difference across each component in parallel is the same
items.misconception: 6 V, since the potential difference of the battery is shared between the two branches
items.why: The sharing rule for series is carried over to parallel, since two components again have to 'divide' something. In parallel it is the current that divides, not the potential difference. Each branch is connected to the same two points, so each has the full supply potential difference.
items.random_wrong: Less than 12 V, since the first lamp has taken some potential difference

items.q: In a parallel circuit one branch carries a current of 0.40 A and the other carries 0.25 A. What is the current in the wire leading from the supply?
items.correct: 0.65 A, the sum of the currents in the two branches
items.misconception: 0.40 A, the same as the current within the larger branch
items.why: The series rule 'same current through each component' is generalised to every circuit, including parallel ones. The same-current rule applies along one path. Where the path divides, the branch currents add to give the total current in the main part of the circuit.
items.random_wrong: 0.15 A, found from the difference of the branch values

items.q: A 20 Ω resistor and a 5 Ω resistor are joined in parallel. Which statement about the total resistance of this pair is correct?
items.correct: It is below 5 Ω, the smaller of the two resistances
items.misconception: It is 25 Ω, the two resistance values added together
items.why: R_total = R_1 + R_2 is memorised as the rule for all combinations, without noticing that it is stated only for series. Adding applies to series only. In parallel the extra branch gives charge another route, so the pair opposes the current less than either resistor alone.
items.random_wrong: It is 12.5 Ω, halfway between the two resistance values

items.q: Explain why connecting a second resistor in series with the first increases the total resistance of the circuit.
items.correct: The charge now has to pass through both resistors in turn, so the single path opposes it more
items.misconception: The second resistor gives the charge another path to follow, and each path opposes it
items.why: The 'extra path' picture belongs to parallel connection and is attached to the series case as well. An extra series resistor lengthens the one path; an extra parallel resistor adds a new path. More path raises resistance, more paths lowers it.
items.random_wrong: The second resistor uses up part of the current before it reaches the first resistor

items.q: Explain why connecting a second resistor in parallel with the first decreases the total resistance of the circuit.
items.correct: The second resistor adds another path, so more charge can flow for the same supply
items.misconception: The two resistance values simply add, and the supply is shared between the branches
items.why: R_total = R_1 + R_2 is memorised as the rule for all combinations, without noticing that it is stated only for series. Adding applies to series only. In parallel the extra branch gives charge another route, so the pair opposes the current less than either resistor alone.
items.random_wrong: The total has to lie between the two values, so it falls below the larger

items.q: Which statement correctly describes a difference between series circuits and parallel circuits?
items.correct: In series the current is the same in each component; in parallel the potential difference is
items.misconception: In series the potential difference is the same across each component; in parallel the current is
items.why: The parallel rule, that the potential difference across each component is the same, is applied to a series circuit. Full supply potential difference across each component is the parallel rule. In series the separate potential differences add up to the supply value.
items.random_wrong: In series the components share out the current; in parallel they share the potential difference

items.q: A student wants to measure the current in a lamp and the potential difference across it. How should the two meters be connected?
items.correct: Ammeter in series with the lamp, voltmeter across its ends
items.misconception: Ammeter in parallel with the lamp, voltmeter in series with it
items.why: Both meters are seen simply as things to add to the circuit, without linking the connection to the quantity being measured. A meter must experience the quantity it reads: the ammeter must carry the lamp's current, so it is in series, and the voltmeter must span the lamp's ends, so it is in parallel.
items.random_wrong: Both of the meters in series with the lamp, one on each side

items.q: A dc series circuit for testing a component contains a cell, an ammeter, a variable resistor and the component, with a voltmeter across the component. Why is the variable resistor included?
items.correct: It changes the current, so several pairs of readings can be taken for the component under test
items.misconception: It keeps the current steady while the potential difference across the component is varied
items.why: The variable resistor is remembered as a control, and 'control' is read as 'keep constant'. Changing its resistance changes the total resistance of the series loop and so changes the current, which is exactly what is wanted to build up a set of readings.
items.random_wrong: It makes the current the same in every part of the circuit while the test is carried out

items.q: A 12 V battery is connected in series with a 3 Ω resistor and a 5 Ω resistor. What is the current in the circuit?
items.correct: 1.5 A, from 12 V divided by the total resistance of 8 Ω
items.misconception: 4 A, from 12 V divided by the 3 Ω resistor on its own
items.why: The resistor being looked at is used in the calculation while the rest of the series loop is forgotten. The current is set by the whole loop. Add the resistances first to get the total, here 8 Ω, then divide the supply potential difference by that total.
items.random_wrong: 6 A, from 12 V divided by the 2 Ω difference of the pair

items.q: A 9 V supply is connected in series with a 2 Ω resistor and a 4 Ω resistor. What is the potential difference across the 4 Ω resistor?
items.correct: 6 V, from the 1.5 A current in the 4 Ω resistor
items.misconception: 9 V, as each component has the whole supply across it
items.why: The parallel rule, that the potential difference across each component is the same, is applied to a series circuit. Full supply potential difference across each component is the parallel rule. In series the separate potential differences add up to the supply value.
items.random_wrong: 4.5 V, as the supply is shared equally between them

items.q: Three 6 Ω resistors are connected in series across a 9 V supply. Using the idea of equivalent resistance, what current does the supply deliver?
items.correct: 0.5 A, using an equivalent resistance of 18 Ω
items.misconception: 1.5 A, using an equivalent resistance of 6 Ω alone
items.why: The idea that the biggest resistance is the bottleneck is borrowed from everyday reasoning about narrow gaps. Every series resistor adds its own opposition, so all of them count. The equivalent resistance is the sum, here 6 Ω + 6 Ω + 6 Ω = 18 Ω.
items.random_wrong: 3 A, using an equivalent resistance of just 3 Ω

items.q: In a circuit a cell is joined to a resistor, and the resistor is joined to two lamps that are placed side by side between the same pair of junctions. How is this circuit best described?
items.correct: It has both kinds of part: the resistor is in series with a parallel pair of lamps
items.misconception: It is a series circuit, because all of the components are joined to one cell
items.why: The two arrangements are first met as opposites, and the pair is taken to be a complete set of choices. Series and parallel describe how any two components are joined, not the whole circuit. Many circuits contain both kinds of connection at once.
items.random_wrong: It is a parallel circuit, because the circuit contains more than one branch

items.q: Three lamps are connected in series with a cell. One lamp is taken out of its holder. What happens to the other two lamps?
items.correct: They both go out, because the single path round the circuit has been broken
items.misconception: They both stay lit, because each lamp has its own path back to the cell
items.why: The independence of parallel branches is remembered as a general fact about circuits with several lamps. Only parallel branches are independent. A series circuit is a single loop, so a gap anywhere stops the current everywhere.
items.random_wrong: They both stay lit but shine brighter, as the total resistance falls

items.q: Two lamps are connected in parallel across a cell. One of the lamps is taken out of its holder. What happens to the remaining lamp?
items.correct: It stays lit as before, since its own branch is still complete
items.misconception: It goes out, since taking one lamp out breaks the circuit
items.why: The series result is applied to every circuit, since removing a lamp is pictured as making a gap in one shared loop. In parallel each branch is a complete path on its own. Breaking one branch leaves the other branch, and its potential difference, unchanged.
items.random_wrong: It shines more brightly, since it now receives all of the current

items.q: A circuit diagram shows a cell, a closed switch and two lamps drawn side by side between the same two junctions. Which measurement would best check that the built circuit matches the diagram?
items.correct: Check that each lamp has the full supply potential difference on it
items.misconception: Check that exactly the same current passes through each of the lamps
items.why: The series rule 'same current through each component' is generalised to every circuit, including parallel ones. The same-current rule applies along one path. Where the path divides, the branch currents add to give the total current in the main part of the circuit.
items.random_wrong: Check that the two lamp potential differences add up to the supply value

items.q: Two components are in series with a cell. Is the current from the cell divided between them?
items.correct: No. In series the same current passes through both components; it is the potential difference that is shared.
items.misconception: The current from the cell splits between the two components, so each gets half of it.
items.why: The word 'shared' is remembered from the potential difference rule and applied to current instead. Current only divides where the path divides, at a junction. A series loop has no junctions, so the same current is in every part of it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A 9 V supply is in series with a 2 Ω and a 4 Ω resistor. How is the potential difference shared?
items.correct: 3 V across the 2 Ω resistor and 6 V across the 4 Ω resistor, since the same current passes through both.
items.misconception: 4.5 V across each, because the supply potential difference is always split equally between the components.
items.why: 'Shared' is read as 'shared equally', ignoring the different resistances of the components. The share depends on resistance. With the same current in both, the larger resistance takes the larger potential difference; the two shares still add to 9 V.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does it matter where in a series loop a component is placed relative to the cell?
items.correct: No. The current is the same through every component, whatever the order of components in the loop.
items.misconception: The component nearest the cell takes more current, leaving less for the ones further round the loop.
items.why: Charge is pictured as a supply of stuff that is handed out along the way, so the first component gets first choice. Current is not handed out along a series loop. The same current passes through every component, so swapping their order changes none of the readings.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Two lamps are in parallel and one is removed. What happens to the other lamp?
items.correct: It stays lit at the same brightness, because it still has the full supply potential difference across its own branch.
items.misconception: It becomes brighter, because it now receives all of the current that the two lamps used to share.
items.why: The supply is imagined to deliver a fixed amount of current that is divided up, rather than a current set by the resistance of each branch. The current in a branch is set by its own resistance and the potential difference across it. Neither changes when the other branch is removed, so the brightness is unchanged.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A voltmeter across the second of two series lamps reads what, if the first already reads 3 V of a 6 V supply?
items.correct: 3 V, because the two shares of the supply potential difference add up to 6 V.
items.misconception: 0 V or nearly nothing, because the first lamp has already used up the potential difference.
items.why: Potential difference is treated as a fuel carried round the loop and spent at the first component reached. Potential difference is not a store that runs out along the way; it is a measure of energy transferred per unit charge at each component. The shares add to the supply value.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do two parallel lamps have the same potential difference only if they are identical?
items.correct: No. The potential difference across each component in parallel is the same whatever their resistances are.
items.misconception: They only have equal potential differences when the two lamps have the same resistance.
items.why: Symmetry is thought to be doing the work, so the rule is believed to fail when the branches differ. The rule follows from the connection, not from the components: both branches end on the same two points, so both have the same potential difference across them.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A 20 Ω and a 5 Ω resistor are in parallel. Where does the total resistance lie?
items.correct: Below 5 Ω, since the total resistance of the pair is less than the smallest individual resistance.
items.misconception: Between 5 Ω and 20 Ω, because a combined value must lie somewhere between the two.
items.why: Averaging is assumed to be the safe answer whenever two values are combined. Adding a parallel branch always makes it easier for charge to flow, so the total falls below even the smallest of the individual resistances.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the variable resistor needed to make the current the same in every part of a series circuit?
items.correct: No. The current is already the same through each component in series, whatever the variable resistor is set to.
items.misconception: The variable resistor is there to even out the current so that every component gets the same amount.
items.why: A job is invented for the component from a property of series circuits that is true for a different reason. Equal current in series follows from there being one path. The variable resistor is added to alter the size of that current, not to make it equal.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In what unit is resistance measured?
items.correct: In ohms, unit symbol Ω, as the specification states: resistance, R, in ohms, Ω.
items.misconception: Resistance is measured in volts, because a voltmeter is used when resistance is investigated.
items.why: The three electrical quantities are met together, and the unit of the one that is easiest to picture is attached to all of them. The volt is the unit of potential difference and the ampere the unit of current. Resistance has its own unit, the ohm, symbol Ω.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Two branches carry 0.40 A and 0.25 A. How are these combined to give the supply current?
items.correct: They are added, giving 0.65 A, because the total current is the sum of the currents through the separate components.
items.misconception: They are subtracted, or averaged, to give the current in the main part of the circuit.
items.why: Any pair of numbers is combined by whichever operation gives a value that looks reasonable, rather than by thinking about charge at a junction. Charge is conserved at a junction: everything that flows in along the branches flows out along the main wire, so the branch currents add.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.2.2 Series and parallel circuits
